(1) NO MINIMUM QUOTE LENGTH and no word-boundary requirement: a single-character quote 'a' is cited against every document, so a degenerate quote is a universal citation. tickets.title: A single-word hub label ending in -s, -ed or -ing SILENTLY DELETES a Meet row's reasoning. Nine of the ten _WHY_PHRASE templates in graph.py put the label directly after a BARE preposition, and digest._reads_as_a_verb treats a capitalised, non-hyphenated, non-ALL-CAPS word ending in s/ed/ing as a verb — so _splices_a_clause fires, is_speakable refuses the line, and _speakable_match falls back to WHY_OF_LAST_RESORT. Traced through the real path (digest._speakable_match), not just the predicate: 'Both connected to Databricks.' -> 'Worth a hello; nothing quotable on the record yet.'; 'Both connected to Reuters.' -> BLANKED; 'Both building on Kubernetes.' -> BLANKED; 'Both deep in Sailing.' -> BLANKED. Databricks, Reuters and Kubernetes are ordinary hub labels for this product's population. Invisible today only because neither corpus contains such a label. The _reads_as_a_verb docstring anticipates the FACT case ('...at Reuters on the data team') and calls rejection 'the safe direction', which is right for a fact — it falls through to the next candidate — but WRONG for a why, where the fallback is not another candidate but an admitted blank. The fix belongs in digest, not graph: a hub label arriving through _WHY_PHRASE is a noun BY CONSTRUCTION, so the why path can tell the verb detector so. Fixing it from graph would mean rewording templates to dodge a downstream heuristic, coupling the two modules and colliding with test_why_phrasing_varies_by_hub_type.
